claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a uniform fcc matrix.
The fcc matrix underpins the alloy's notable strength and fatigue performance.
Selective oxidation kinetics primarily governs degradation of this alloy during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases.
Oxygen diffusion through an evolving multi-element oxide scale determines whether the scale is protective and continuous or non-protective and cracked.
The combined actions of Al, Cr, and Ti control oxygen diffusion and oxide-scale evolution.
Exposure at 850–950°C produces oxide scales whose thickness, morphology, and composition vary with oxygen partial pressure.
The surface scales may contain aluminates, chromites, or mixed oxides.
At high oxygen partial pressure, rapid oxygen diffusion produces a thick, continuous, protective multi-element oxide scale.
The thick protective scale formed at high oxygen partial pressure limits subsequent degradation through diffusion-controlled, self-limiting oxidation.
Under reducing conditions, limited oxygen availability produces thin, poorly adherent, or cracked oxide scales.
Thin, poorly adherent, or cracked scales under reducing conditions accelerate degradation.
Reducing-atmosphere exposure will cause more scale cracking or spallation than high-oxygen exposure.
Reducing-atmosphere exposure will produce accelerated degradation relative to the unexposed starting-state baseline.
The unexposed as-built alloy has minimal pre-existing oxide and an intact fcc matrix.
The proposed oxygen-diffusion mechanism applies primarily between 850°C and 950°C in oxygen-partial-pressure regimes dominated by diffusion-controlled oxidation.
Outside the specified temperature and oxygen-partial-pressure regime, degradation mechanisms such as thermal-mechanical stresses from cycling may predominate.
